terms.comment: First a commander, and the title soldiers gave a victorious general; from Augustus on a title of the emperors, and then the plain word for an emperor (Lewis & Short). Traupman and Morgan–Owens use it for any emperor, of China too (Wolff, 1726). An empress is imperātrix (Levi–Bini p. 33), a rare word in antiquity.

The title Augustus chose: he took the state, worn out by civil war, under his power nōmine prīncipis (Tac. Ann. 1.1). The usual word for the emperor in Tacitus and Pliny; Lewis & Short call this sense poetic and post-Augustan.
Julius Caesar’s family name, borne by every emperor after him (Lewis & Short); Morgan–Owens gives it for the emperors who claimed the Roman succession.

phrases.latin: posse etiam sub malīs prīncipibus magnōs virōs esse
phrases.english: that there can be great men even under bad emperors

phrases.latin: psittacus ā vōbīs aliōrum nōmina discam: hoc didicī per mē dīcere «Caesar, havē»
phrases.english: I, the parrot, shall learn other names from you; this I learned to say by myself: “Hail, Caesar!”
